passage: "Sign here, and we can settle this quickly," the officer said, sliding a paper across the desk. The station smelled of old tea and dust. I'm Jyoti, and I'd only gone in after a minor scooter accident. He tapped the page, then rubbed two fingers together and said, "A small amount, and it all goes away." My palms were sweating and my mind said, just do it, just leave. But I looked at the paper and couldn't read half the words. I said, "I don't sign what I haven't understood. I'd like my brother here, or a lawyer." His face hardened. I kept my voice level and wrote down his name and badge number. Then I rang my friend Rehana, who was a law student, and she came straight over. I never signed.

qa.q: What did the officer slide across the desk?
qa.a: He slid a paper across the desk.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as the officer pushed the paper?
qa.a: Frightened and tempted to give in, since Jyoti's palms were sweating and a voice said to just do it and leave.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that protected Jyoti?
qa.a: Jyoti refused to sign what was not understood, asked for a brother or a lawyer, noted the name and badge number, and called Rehana.

qa.q: How might the officer have seen Jyoti's refusal?
qa.a: As an unwelcome obstacle, since his face hardened when Jyoti did not simply comply.

grounding: An officer presses for money and a signature; the protagonist refuses to sign what has not been read, asks for a family member or lawyer and notes names.

passage:
Wednesday. Thomas's scooter had scraped a parked car outside the Ernakulam market. Nobody was hurt. At the police post, the officer pushed a typed paper towards him. "Sign, and it's settled. Or pay five thousand and go." The paper was in small print. Thomas's heart hammered. He said, "I'd like to read it first and call my family." He noted the officer's name tag and the time.

Thursday. His aunt Dilnaz came with him. She read the paper slowly. It said he admitted to reckless driving. Thomas went cold. She asked the officer to explain it and asked for a copy. The officer's tone changed.

The following Monday. Through a lawyer she knew, they settled it properly with the car owner and got a receipt for the repair. Thomas kept the officer's name and the times in a notebook, in case he needed to complain.

qa.q: What did the paper say Thomas admitted to?
qa.a: It said he admitted to reckless driving.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when the officer pushed the paper towards him?
qa.a: Thomas felt frightened and pressured, with his heart hammering, but stayed calm enough to ask for time.

qa.q: Why was refusing to sign right away the wise choice?
qa.a: The paper was in small print and turned out to admit reckless driving, so asking to read it and call family protected Thomas.

qa.q: How might the officer's view have changed when Dilnaz arrived?
qa.a: The officer seemed less confident once an adult read the paper carefully and asked questions, which is why his tone changed.

grounding: The three beats show a young man pressed to sign an unread paper or pay money, refusing, calling family and noting names and times.

passage:
Kalyani, listen to your Uday uncle's story before you go off to that job in the city. When I was twenty-one, I rode my cycle to the night shift at the sugar factory. One night a constable stopped me at the crossing. He said my cycle had no light, and it didn't, that part was true. Then he said, "Two hundred rupees, or I take you to the station and you'll lose your job."

My legs shook. Two hundred was half my week. I nearly paid.

But I remembered my father's words: never pay or sign in a panic. I said, "Sir, I'll come to the station. Please let me call my father first." I read his name badge aloud, slowly, so he knew I'd seen it.

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he said, "Get a light by tomorrow," and walked off. I bought the light. And I wrote his name in my diary.

qa.q: What was missing from young Uday's cycle?
How did young Uday feel when the constable demanded money?
qa.a: Young Uday felt frightened, with shaking legs, and nearly paid out of panic.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed the outcome?
qa.a: Uday refused to pay in a panic, asked to call his father, and read the constable's name aloud, so the constable backed off.

qa.q: How might the constable have seen Uday after he read the name badge?
qa.a: The constable probably realised Uday was not easy to pressure and might report him, so he let him go.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young man pressed for money by an officer who stays calm, asks to call family and notes the officer's name.
